correctness.rationale: For finite downward-closed languages, singular substitution of ↓w by ↓z equals ↓h_z(w), proved by decomposition into chosen or omitted source letter-blocks. Left quotient by c of ↓w is the principal ideal generated by the suffix after the earliest c, or empty if absent. Unique maximal-generator antichains make this a complete deterministic quotient calculus. The explicit certificate lists 15, 8 and 127 distinct, reachable canonical states, all their 300 transitions and their closures, and a standalone checker verifies each entry. Unique antichains separate all states, giving matching upper and lower bounds on κ, not merely sampled lengths. A separately implemented epsilon-NFA construction determinizes to 337 subsets and minimizes to 127 states. Exact inequality 127>15·8=120. Scope: binary finite languages and the usual complete DFA state complexity.

originality.rationale: Guyot arXiv:2407.10355v1, Conjecture 3.25 explicitly asserts the product bound for arbitrary downward-closed languages. The newly specified overlapping-alphabet two-generator witness violates it. Proposition 3.7 needs both inputs principal, Theorem 3.22 requires disjoint alphabets, and Theorem 3.27 requires a source that is a product of atoms; these do not imply the contested statement in this case. An author-hosted later indexed version still presents the conjecture. No equivalent bound-refuting 15,8,127 case was found in searches; unindexed priority remains possible.

value.rationale: A published explicit universal conjecture about the state complexity of singular substitution is falsified by a transparent binary example: the substitute ideal is principal and the source is merely a union of two incomparable principal ideals. This identifies a sharp qualitative boundary for extensions of proven disjoint-alphabet/directness hypotheses, relevant to compositional automata sizes for downward-closed languages. It is not justified by a small isolated numerical increment but by falsity of the asserted general theorem. No optimality of the witness or superquadratic asymptotics is asserted.
